title: Rav Pinchas
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was a student of Rava, as we find that he always said [teachings] in his name: Shabbat 46b; Yevamot 29b; Gittin 83b; Nedarim 73b; Niddah 46b.

And we find in Chagigah 26a, "he said in the name of Rav," which Hyman says must be corrected to "in the name of Rava," as in Bava Metzia 62a. The statement is cited in Bava Kamma 54b and Sanhedrin 85a, where the words "in the name of Rava" are missing; and in Yevamot 22b the statement is said in the name of Rav Pappa.

So too it is mentioned in Moed Katan 14b: Amemar, and if you wish, Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi, taught thus: Rav Pinchas said, "We too have learned [a teaching]" and Rav Ashi raised a difficulty against him; and in Shevuot 22a he resolves the words of Rav Pappa. From all this Hyman concludes that he was a Babylonian in the generation of Rava and Rav Pappa. Hyman therefore argues that it is impossible to say, as the introduction to the Yerushalmi holds, that Rav Pinchas, Rava's student, went up to the Land of Israel, since by then the academies of the Land of Israel had already been destroyed, as he himself says there on p. 117. And Rabbi Pinchas who is always mentioned in the Yerushalmi is a different Amora.

notes.text: The Rav/Rava/Rav Pappa readings and the argument against identifying this sage with the Yerushalmi Rabbi Pinchas are Hyman’s source comparisons.

Shabbat 46b directly has Pinchas reporting Rava. Hyman’s always wording, Rav/Rava/Rav Pappa comparisons, impossible-migration argument and distinction from the Jerusalem Talmud Pinchas remain his conclusions, not newly established destruction history or authority identities.
